Before the city wakes, there is an hour when the world seems to belong to no one. A bicycle ticks past the bakery. Pigeons gather on a windowsill, solemn as committee members. Somewhere, a kettle begins its song.

I like this hour because nothing in it asks to be impressive. The sky does not perform a sunrise; it simply loosens the dark. Bread becomes fragrant behind a door. A gardener lifts one fallen branch from the path and carries on.

Most days, I move through life as though it were a corridor leading somewhere else. I measure the present by its usefulness: what it finishes, what it proves, what it makes possible next. But attention has a different arithmetic. It finds abundance in things that cannot be accumulated.

Consider a cup of tea. Leaves have traveled farther than I will today. Water has been cloud, river, ice, and mist. Hands I will never meet have shaped the cup, planted the leaves, repaired the pipes. Even solitude turns out to be crowded with quiet generosity.

This does not make every moment meaningful, nor should it. Some moments are only dull, and some are genuinely hard. Still, there is relief in looking without demanding a lesson. The world is not always a message. Sometimes it is only rain tapping the glass, a sock warming on the radiator, a stranger laughing in another room.

For once, that is enough. The hour passes. The city clears its throat. I begin again, slightly more here.
